annotations.text:
THE CHARITY — all seven flow steps

A fundraising director who uses this twice a month and is not a compliance specialist.

Three of these do not exist today: the first run (their first screen is currently an unstyled password box), the concern they have raised going anywhere, and any view across more than one audit.

Every screen opens with the answer to the question they arrived with — usually 'nothing needs you' — then lets them read down for why.

2 · BOOK

S3.2 folded in as a step rather than a separate screen: choose anyone eligible, or somebody specific by code.

The hard block is explained where it happens — a conflicted auditor is not a setting you can override, and the copy says why rather than just refusing.

3 · YOUR AUDITS

Grouped by what it means to them — ready, under way, waiting for an auditor, finished — rather than listed by our status enum.

Only one group has an action in it. The rest are there to stop them worrying.

6 · RAISING A CONCERN — NEW

Today a charity types into a box and never hears anything again.

This gives the concern a life: acknowledged, being investigated, one of three named outcomes. It also explains, once, why they are not talking to the auditor directly — because that is the product working, not us being obstructive.

7 · ACROSS AUDITS — NEW

Flow map finding 04: every audit is an island, and this is the question that decides whether they renew.

The pattern is the product. One report says a fundraiser did something wrong; four say the agency has a training problem and it started in July.

All the data exists. Nothing reads across it.

THE AUDITOR — all eleven flow steps

A contractor, outdoors, one-handed, often with no signal — and during the mystery shop they must not be seen using this at all.

Four do not exist today: what happens while they wait to be approved, declaring a conflict when accepting, arriving, and being told their write-up came back.

Portal screens are 1000px; field screens are at real phone width, 414px.

1 · THE INVITATION — rebuilt twice

The version we shipped last week asks its questions before answering any of theirs, and it asks the hardest one badly.

COVERAGE IS NOW A TRAVEL QUESTION. 'Postcode areas you cover' made an auditor translate 'how far will I go' into geography they would have to look up. Nobody thinks in postcode areas. They think '45 minutes on the tube' or 'an hour in the car'.

So: base postcode, how far, and how they travel — then we DERIVE the areas and show them, editable. The auditor checks a list rather than composing one.

MODE IS NOT JUST A DISTANCE MULTIPLIER. An hour by car in rural Scotland is a different world from an hour on the tube, and only a driver reaches a retail park with no station. It is a capability, like av_capable.

WHAT THIS COSTS: nothing at match time. Matching stays a join on postcode_area — the derivation happens once, on save, against a static table of the 121 UK postcode areas. The travel radius work deferred in FUNCTIONALITY stays deferred; we just stop making the auditor do it in their head.

Store BOTH: max_travel_minutes and travel_mode on auditor_profile, plus the derived rows in auditor_coverage. If we ever want real journey times, the inputs are already captured — which is the standing rule about recording everything from day one.

5 · ACCEPTING — NEW conflict step

The database blocks a conflict PICK already knows about. A friend on that agency's team is invisible to us, and nothing today invites the auditor to say so.

Independence is the product, so this is the moment to ask — and the copy makes declaring one costless, because an auditor who fears losing work will not.

7 · ARRIVING — NEW

Today 'start session' means both 'I am here' and 'the audit is running', and the 45-minute no-show clock runs from it — so an auditor who arrives early and waits properly is penalised for pressing it late.

Two buttons, two facts.

8 · WORKING THE SHIFT

The highest-stakes screen in the product: read at arm's length, in daylight, while watching something you cannot pause.

Counters are the whole interface during the watching half. The screen says what is coming BEFORE it arrives, so nobody is surprised into holding a phone during the mystery shop.

10 · SENT BACK — NEW

Nobody is told today. The work waits on someone who does not know it is waiting.

It leads with reassurance because the first thought is 'am I in trouble' and the second is 'do I still get paid' — and the answers are no and yes. Only the moments PICK unlocked are editable; the other 27 are visibly locked.

VERDICT FIRST, THEN READ DOWN

Applied to all 18 screens. Each opens with the one thing the person came for — in words, not a number — then lets them read down a sequence for the evidence.

IT ONLY WORKS WHERE BOTH ARE TRUE:

· the system HAS a judgement
· the content HAS a real order

Where there is no judgement, the opening line still answers the question they arrived with — which is often 'nothing needs you'. That is a verdict too, and it is the most valuable one on a waiting screen.

WHERE IT DOES NOT APPLY

The assignment console (S4.2) fails both tests: six parallel eligibility rules, no chronology, and PICK is choosing rather than being told. Forcing a timeline onto it would be worse than the flat list it has now. The ops queue (S4.1) takes the verdict half only — it is ranked, not sequential.

THE EIGHT MOMENTS ARE THE SPINE

Approach · Walk-up · Opening · Pitch · Ask · Tablet · Sign-up · Close

They appear in the same order, with the same names, on the report, the prep cards, the session and the write-up. A charity and an auditor end up describing the same shift the same way — which is most of what makes two apps feel like one product.

WHAT I INVENTED — CHECK THESE

1. THE VERDICT WORDS. The product says PASS and FAIL. These say 'in order' and 'breach' to a charity, and ask an auditor Yes / No / Note — because the checks are written as questions and 'did they stop asking? FAIL' reads backwards. A real change to core, not layout.

2. EVERY TIMING PROMISE. 'Two or three working days' for vetting, 'report expected Monday', 'next payout run is Friday 5 September', 'we will let you know'. The product has no SLAs, no schedule and no notifications. Every screen here quietly assumes all three.

3. 'WHY THIS CHECK MATTERS' lines, on the report, prep and rework. Not a field that exists — it would be a client-facing note on check_definition.

4. THE ARRIVAL BRIEF — where they stand, what the tabards look like. Captured nowhere today.

5. TIME ESTIMATES on offers ('about 90 min') and the write-up ('about ten minutes left'). Reasonable, unmeasured.

6. THE HISTORY SCREEN'S RECURRENCE ANALYSIS. The data exists; nothing computes it. It is the biggest single build here.

7. 'You have passed on 3 offers this month · that is fine' — I invented both the counter and the reassurance. Worth deciding whether we track that at all, because an auditor who feels counted behaves differently.

8. Jaz named as account manager and jaz@pick.example. Placeholders.

IF YOU BUILD ONE THING FROM THIS

Notifications. Not a screen — the absence underneath half of these designs.

Six of the eighteen say some version of 'we will let you know', and none of them can. An offer expiring in four hours, a report going live, a write-up coming back, vetting finishing: all silent today.

The screens work without it. The product does not.

PICK — the third actor

Two people running a marketplace. Everything has to be dispatchable in one pass, and nothing may be silently dropped.

THE PATTERN BENDS HERE, DELIBERATELY. A charity and an auditor arrive with a question and want an answer. PICK arrives with a LIST and wants it empty. So the verdict half stays — every screen opens with what needs a person — but the sequence half only applies where there genuinely is one (a payout run, an advisory trail). Forcing a timeline onto the assignment console would be worse than the table it deserves.

All eight of these exist today. None is a new screen; what changes is what each one leads with.

2 · WHO CAN DO THIS

The screen the flow map said fails both tests — six parallel eligibility rules, no chronology. So it gets a table, not a timeline.

The design work is making the SIX SETS legible as columns, so the first failing one is the thing to fix — and pairing each near-miss with the action that would clear it ('sign off?', 'widen?'). Today it is a flat list of who qualified.

Exposure warns; conflict never waives. Both are said once, at the bottom, rather than repeated in every row.

3 · REVIEWING A WRITE-UP

The two gates resolve SEPARATELY on screen, which is TND-79 made visible: the auditor was paid on submission and nothing here changes that.

It also surfaces what the auditor flagged LIVE during the shift, with times, beside their written findings. A critical breach corroborated at 14:22 is a different thing from one remembered afterwards — and that is exactly what a reviewer should be weighing.

5 · A CONCERN — NEW triage

TND-80's three paths made concrete: the finding stands, ask the auditor for more, or uphold it and re-audit at our cost.

The reply box says 'nothing here reaches the auditor'. That separation IS the product — an auditor whose findings can be argued with by the charity paying for them is not independent — so the screen states it where the decision gets made.

The corroboration panel also caught something real: the charity has read 'followed' into a finding about persistence. Worth correcting in the reply.

WHAT I INVENTED HERE

1. THE COVERAGE GAP on Today — 'nobody covers SE for lottery'. Nothing computes this. It is probably the single most useful thing a marketplace operator can be told, and it is a real build.

2. 'Approve unlocks when the agreement is in' on vetting. There is no agreement-tracking field. Given TND-58 gates going live, there probably should be.

3. Auto-release timers — 'releases in 2 days if nobody looks'. The gate stores timeout_days and nothing applies it; there is no scheduler. TND-81.

4. 'No finding overturned in 4 audits' on triage. We do not track overturn history.

5. Every count of what a charity has spent, and breaches found. Derivable, not derived.

6. The CSV export on a past run. TND-94, not built.

11–12 · WHERE YOU WILL WORK

The hardest question in onboarding, and the one the first version got wrong twice.

V1 asked for postcode areas — geography an auditor has to look up. V2 asked for travel time and then showed them postcode areas anyway, which is the same problem wearing a hat.

THE FIX IS TO STOP SHOWING CODES AT ALL. An auditor says where they start, how long they will travel and how. We propose PLACES — Salford, Trafford, Stockport — and they tick or untick. Place names are the one geographic unit every country has.

The screen is honest that the times are as the crow flies, because a river or a bad junction will make one wrong. Untick is the correction, and we keep it.

The artboard beside this is why the schema has to move first: today an audit's postcode is checked against a UK regex, so the product cannot store a Dublin address at all.
